findings.evidence: template/scripts/publication_queue.py: `_transition` now uses `if state in ATTENTION_STATES: ensure_attention(...)`. `ensure_attention` wraps a failed POST as `AttentionError` (around line 773). `_integration_repair` (around lines 2361-2372) calls `_transition` and then `publish_job` under `except LifecycleOwnershipChanged` / `except QueueError` only. The `worker` loop catches `(QueueError, WorkerError, RequirementIntegrationError, GitCommandError)`, not `AttentionError`. Posting the attention comment after `publish_job`, or catching `AttentionError` on the repair paths, would keep a comment failure from blocking job publication.
findings.summary: `_transition` now calls `ensure_attention` for `repair-pending` and `integration-repair-pending`. When the comment POST fails, `ensure_attention` raises `AttentionError`, which is a `RuntimeError` and not a `QueueError`. In `_integration_repair`, `_transition` runs before `publish_job`, and the `except QueueError` there does not catch it. Nothing in `worker` catches it either. A transient GitHub error on the new escalation comment therefore aborts the whole queue run. The `ACTIVE` label has already been released and the record is written, but the repair job is not published until a later pass recovers it. Before this change only `blocked-escalation` could raise this error, and a block is terminal. The new repair-state escalation sits on the job-publication path.
